title: Between standing and lying
hookLine: the night before the council, Ananda gives up striving, lies down, and is freed before his head reaches the pillow (Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
carry: before his head reached the pillow

cards: A deadline, and a sacred one. The elders are gathering at Rajagaha to recite the teaching together, and in the Vinaya's account every one of them has already reached the end of the path.
Every one except Ananda: the man who walked beside the Buddha, carried his water, heard the discourses day after day. So on the last night he does the obvious thing with a deadline.
He works, attending to the body hour after hour, pushing at a door that won't open. Then, toward dawn, he stops pushing. He decides to lie down.

teach.b: First, the push. The Vinaya says Ananda spent much of that night in mindfulness of the body. This isn't a lazy man looking for a shortcut; it's a careful one, practicing the way he was taught.
And still, by effort alone, nothing gives. Second, the letting go.

teach.h: HE LET GO, AND LAY DOWN.
teach.b: Toward dawn he thinks: let me lie down. He isn't quitting the path, only setting down the strain. A later commentary adds a reason: he saw that his effort had grown too tight, and he eased it.

teach.h: BEFORE HIS HEAD TOUCHED THE PILLOW.
teach.b: He leans his body toward the bed, and the text says that before his head reached the pillow, while his feet had not yet left the ground, his mind was freed. Not sitting, not walking, not lying down. Somewhere in between.
The thing he had chased so long came in a moment that doesn't even have a name. Fourth, what it says. Ananda didn't stop practicing; his long practice was the ground under his feet.
What he stopped was the clutching. The story doesn't say effort is useless.
It says effort can tighten into a fist, and a closed fist can't receive anything.
In the morning, the account goes on, he took his place among the elders as one of them.

how: Teachers in several Buddhist traditions tell Ananda's last night as a story about balanced effort, and recall it for students whose practice has grown tight and forced.

o: a monk who keeps the strictest practices
a senior monk who presides at a council
one who has reached the end of the path

s: that night Ananda gave up the path
he set down the strain, not the practice; in the morning he joined the elders as one of them.
he was freed while sitting in meditation
it came as he leaned down to rest, before his head reached the pillow.
Ananda spent much of that night in mindfulness of the body
the Vinaya says he practiced hard that night; the release came only when he set the strain down.

games.q: you're Ananda. it's nearly dawn, the council is tomorrow, and pushing hasn't worked. what do you do?
o: set down the strain and lie down.
games.why: he decides to lie down, and before his head reaches the pillow his mind is freed. the release comes when the clutching stops.

practice: Notice where you're pushing right now: the jaw, the shoulders, the space between the eyebrows, maybe even the breath, being managed.

Let one of those go, the way Ananda let himself lie down; you're only setting down the extra, and if you catch yourself working hard at relaxing, smile at it. Then stay with the breath as it is, without trying to improve it.

wordCard.voice: Arahant. What Ananda becomes the night before the council, freed between standing and lying, before his head reaches the pillow. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali arahant: one who has reached the end of the path, as the elders of the council had.

carryVoice: Your line: before his head reached the pillow. What he chased came when the clutching stopped. Rest easy.
